claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers under sustained loading is governed by the evolution of interfacial dislocation structures.
Evolving interfacial dislocation structures enable localized shear softening.
Compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order differences magnify the difference in dislocation mobility between alternating FCC and BCC HEA layers.
A mismatch in dislocation mobility causes geometrically necessary dislocations to accumulate at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations produces a plasticity gradient.
The resulting plasticity gradient is the rate-limiting mechanism in creep deformation.
The proposed starting material consists of alternating FCC and BCC HEA layers with chemically distinct interfaces.
Differential dislocation mobility causes preferential accumulation of dislocations at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial dislocation accumulation leads to localized shear-band formation.
Localized shear bands progressively facilitate plastic deformation under sustained loading.
Nanoscale layering accentuates interfacial dislocation accumulation and localization relative to a uniform microstructure.
Sustained loading will increase dislocation concentration at layer interfaces relative to the initial state.
Sustained loading will produce localized shear bands at layer interfaces.
FCC/BCC HEA multilayers will exhibit a higher creep rate than homogeneous single-phase HEA films of similar overall chemistry and thickness.
FCC/BCC HEA multilayers will exhibit more pronounced plastic-strain localization than homogeneous single-phase HEA films.
The proposed mechanism applies while nanoscale layering is maintained and loading activates dislocation glide without causing premature failure.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply if interfaces degrade or film morphology changes significantly.
